draft.title: Sedentary behaviour
card: Sedentary behaviour is time spent sitting or lying down while awake, using very little energy. Watching TV, using a phone, sitting in class and travelling by car are examples.
Sleeping is not sedentary behaviour, because the person is not awake. Standing and walking are not sedentary either.
Long periods of sitting can harm health, even for people who also exercise. Time spent being active does not cancel out the time spent sitting.
Breaking up sitting time with short bursts of movement, such as standing up or walking, can help reduce the harm.
draft.remember: Sitting for long periods can harm health, even if you also exercise.

a.q: Which of these is an example of sedentary behaviour?
opts: Scrolling on a phone while sitting on the couch
Sleeping for eight hours overnight
Walking to the bus stop after school
Standing at a bench to cook dinner
a.why: Sitting on a couch while awake uses very little energy, so it is sedentary. Sleeping is lying down, but the person is not awake, so it does not count.
a.clue: Look for a person who is awake and sitting or lying.

b.q: Ravi trains at the gym for an hour each morning. He then sits at a desk and at home on screens for most of the day. What does this show about his health?
opts: His long sitting time can still harm his health
His gym session fully cancels out the harm of sitting
His sitting is harmless because he is fit and active
His sitting only counts if he skips his gym session
b.why: Exercise does not cancel out long periods of sitting, so Ravi's sitting time can still harm his health. The tempting answer says his training protects him fully, but the card says time being active does not remove the effect of time sitting.
b.clue: Does time spent exercising erase the time spent sitting?

a.best: Scrolling on a phone while sitting on the couch

b.best: His long sitting time can still harm his health

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('can still'), while every wrong option is an absolute ('fully', 'harmless', 'only'). A student could pick it by avoiding absolutes without knowing the idea.

'Time spent being active does not cancel out the time spent sitting' is stated as absolute. Research (e.g. Ekelund et al., 2016) suggests high levels of moderate-vigorous activity (about 60 to 75 minutes a day) may greatly reduce or remove the extra mortality risk of high sitting time. Wording such as 'does not fully cancel out for most people' would be safer.

check.summary: Both answers are correct and the card is accurate overall. Question b's right option stands out as the only hedged choice. The card's claim that activity never cancels out sitting is stronger than the research supports.
